question: In immunizing school entrants with BCG, you are not obliged to secure parental consent. This is because of which legal document?
rationale: P.D. 996. Presidential Decree 996, enacted in 1976, made immunization in the EPI compulsory for children under 8 years of age. Hepatitis B vaccination was made compulsory for the same age group by R.A. 7846.

question: Which immunization produces a permanent scar?
rationale: BCG. BCG causes the formation of a superficial abscess, which begins 2 weeks after immunization. The abscess heals without treatment, with the formation of a permanent scar.

question: A 4-week old baby was brought to the health center for his first immunization. Which can be given to him?
rationale: Infant BCG. Infant BCG may be given at birth. All the other immunizations mentioned can be given at 6 weeks of age.

question: You will not give DPT 2 if the mother says that the infant had

choices.D: Local tenderness for 3 days after DPT 1.

rationale: Seizures a day after DPT 1. Seizures within 3 days after administration of DPT is an indication of hypersensitivity to pertussis vaccine, a component of DPT. This is considered a specific contraindication to subsequent doses of DPT.

question: A 2-month old infant was brought to the health center for immunization. During assessment, the infant’s temperature registered at 38.1°C. Which is the best course of action that you will take?

choices.A: Go on with the infant’s immunizations.
choices.B: Give Paracetamol and wait for his fever to subside.
choices.C: Refer the infant to the physician for further assessment.
choices.D: dvise the infant’s mother to bring him back for immunization when he is well.

rationale: Go on with the infant’s immunizations. In the EPI, fever up to 38.5°C is not a contraindication to immunization. Mild acute respiratory tract infection, simple diarrhea and malnutrition are not contraindications either.

question: A pregnant woman had just received her 4th dose of tetanus toxoid. Subsequently, her baby will have protection against tetanus for how long?
rationale: 1 year. The baby will have passive natural immunity by placental transfer of antibodies. The mother will have active artificial immunity lasting for about 10 years. 5 doses will give the mother lifetime protection.

question: A 4-month old infant was brought to the health center because of cough. Her respiratory rate is 42/minute. Using the Integrated Management of Child Illness (IMCI) guidelines of assessment, her breathing is considered
rationale: Normal. In IMCI, a respiratory rate of 50/minute or more is fast breathing for an infant aged 2 to 12 months.

question: Which of the following signs will indicate that a young child is suffering from severe pneumonia?
rationale: Chest indrawing. In IMCI, chest indrawing is used as the positive sign of dyspnea, indicating severe pneumonia.

question: Using IMCI guidelines, you classify a child as having severe pneumonia. What is the best management for the child?

choices.B: Refer him urgently to the hospital.
choices.C: Instruct the mother to increase fluid intake.
choices.D: Instruct the mother to continue breastfeeding.

rationale: Refer him urgently to the hospital. Severe pneumonia requires urgent referral to a hospital. Answers A, C and D are done for a client classified as having pneumonia.

question: A 5-month old infant was brought by his mother to the health center because of diarrhea occurring 4 to 5 times a day. His skin goes back slowly after a skin pinch and his eyes are sunken. Using the IMCI guidelines, you will classify this infant in which category?
rationale: Some dehydration. Using the assessment guidelines of IMCI, a child (2 months to 5 years old) with diarrhea is classified as having SOME DEHYDRATION if he shows 2 or more of the following signs: restless or irritable, sunken eyes, the skin goes back slow after a skin pinch.

question: Based on assessment, you classified a 3-month old infant with the chief complaint of diarrhea in the category of SOME DEHYDRATION. Based on IMCI management guidelines, which of the following will you do?

choices.A: ring the infant to the nearest facility where IV fluids can be given.
choices.B: Supervise the mother in giving 200 to 400 ml. of Oresol in 4 hours.
choices.C: Give the infant’s mother instructions on home management.
choices.D: Keep the infant in your health center for close observation.

rationale: Supervise the mother in giving 200 to 400 ml. of Oresol in 4 hours. In the IMCI management guidelines, SOME DEHYDRATION is treated with the administration of Oresol within a period of 4 hours. The amount of Oresol is best computed on the basis of the child’s weight (75 ml/kg body weight). If the weight is unknown, the amount of Oresol is based on the child’s age.

question: A mother is using Oresol in the management of diarrhea of her 3-year old child. She asked you what to do if her child vomits. You will tell her to

choices.A: ring the child to the nearest hospital for further assessment.
choices.B: ring the child to the health center for intravenous fluid therapy.
choices.C: ring the child to the health center for assessment by the physician.
choices.D: Let the child rest for 10 minutes then continue giving Oresol more slowly.

rationale: Let the child rest for 10 minutes then continue giving Oresol more slowly. If the child vomits persistently, that is, he vomits everything that he takes in, he has to be referred urgently to a hospital. Otherwise, vomiting is managed by letting the child rest for 10 minutes and then continuing with Oresol administration. Teach the mother to give Oresol more slowly.

question: A 1 ½ year old child was classified as having 3rd degree protein energy malnutrition, kwashiorkor. Which of the following signs will be most apparent in this child?
rationale: Edema. Edema, a major sign of kwashiorkor, is caused by decreased colloidal osmotic pressure of the blood brought about by hypoalbuminemia. Decreased blood albumin level is due a protein-deficient diet.

question: Assessment of a 2-year old child revealed “baggy pants”. Using the IMCI guidelines, how will you manage this child?

choices.A: Refer the child urgently to a hospital for confinement.
choices.B: oordinate with the social worker to enroll the child in a feeding program.
choices.C: Make a teaching plan for the mother, focusing on menu planning for her child.
choices.D: ssess and treat the child for health problems like infections and intestinal parasitism.

rationale: Refer the child urgently to a hospital for confinement. “Baggy pants” is a sign of severe marasmus. The best management is urgent referral to a hospital.

question: During the physical examination of a young child, what is the earliest sign of xerophthalmia that you may observe?
rationale: Conjunctival xerosis. The earliest sign of Vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia) is night blindness. However, this is a functional change, which is not observable during physical examination.The earliest visible lesion is conjunctival xerosis or dullness of the conjunctiva due to inadequate tear production.

question: To prevent xerophthalmia, young children are given Retinol capsule every 6 months. What is the dose given to preschoolers?
rationale: 200,000 IU. Preschoolers are given Retinol 200,000 IU every 6 months. 100,000 IU is given once to infants aged 6 to 12 months. The dose for pregnant women is 10,000 IU.

question: The major sign of iron deficiency anemia is pallor. What part is best examined for pallor?
rationale: Palms. The anatomic characteristics of the palms allow a reliable and convenient basis for examination for pallor.

question: Food fortification is one of the strategies to prevent micronutrient deficiency conditions. R.A. 8976 mandates fortification of certain food items. Which of the following is among these food items?
rationale: Sugar. R.A. 8976 mandates fortification of rice, wheat flour, sugar and cooking oil with Vitamin A, iron and/or iodine.

question: What is the best course of action when there is a measles epidemic in a nearby municipality?

choices.A: Give measles vaccine to babies aged 6 to 8 months.
choices.B: Give babies aged 6 to 11 months one dose of 100,000 I.U. of Retinol
choices.C: Instruct mothers to keep their babies at home to prevent disease transmission.
choices.D: Instruct mothers to feed their babies adequately to enhance their babies’ resistance.

rationale: Give measles vaccine to babies aged 6 to 8 months. Ordinarily, measles vaccine is given at 9 months of age. During an impending epidemic, however, one dose may be given to babies aged 6 to 8 months. The mother is instructed that the baby needs another dose when the baby is 9 months old.

question: A mother brought her daughter, 4 years old, to the RHU because of cough and colds. Following the IMCI assessment guide, which of the following is a danger sign that indicates the need for urgent referral to a hospital?
rationale: Inability to drink. A sick child aged 2 months to 5 years must be referred urgently to a hospital if he/she has one or more of the following signs: not able to feed or drink, vomits everything, convulsions, abnormally sleepy or difficult to awaken.

question: Management of a child with measles includes the administration of which of the following?

choices.C: Tetracycline eye ointment for corneal opacity
choices.D: Retinol capsule regardless of when the last dose was given

rationale: Retinol capsule regardless of when the last dose was given. An infant 6 to 12 months classified as a case of measles is given Retinol 100,000 IU; a child is given 200,000 IU regardless of when the last dose was given.

question: A mother brought her 10 month old infant for consultation because of fever, which started 4 days prior to consultation. To determine malaria risk, what will you do?

choices.C: Get a specimen for blood smear.
choices.D: sk if the fever is present everyday.

rationale: Ask where the family resides. Because malaria is endemic, the first question to determine malaria risk is where the client’s family resides. If the area of residence is not a known endemic area, ask if the child had traveled within the past 6 months, where he/she was brought and whether he/she stayed overnight in that area.

question: The following are strategies implemented by the Department of Health to prevent mosquito-borne diseases. Which of these is most effective in the control of Dengue fever?

choices.C: hemoprophylaxis of non-immune persons going to endemic areas
choices.D: Teaching people in endemic areas to use chemically treated mosquito nets

rationale: Destroying breeding places of mosquitoes. Aedes aegypti, the vector of Dengue fever, breeds in stagnant, clear water. Its feeding time is usually during the daytime. It has a cyclical pattern of occurrence, unlike malaria which is endemic in certain parts of the country.

question: Secondary prevention for malaria includes

choices.A: Planting of neem or eucalyptus trees
choices.B: Residual spraying of insecticides at night
choices.C: etermining whether a place is endemic or not
choices.D: Growing larva-eating fish in mosquito breeding places

rationale: Determining whether a place is endemic or not. This is diagnostic and therefore secondary level prevention. The other choices are for primary prevention.

question: Scotch tape swab is done to check for which intestinal parasite?
rationale: Pinworm. Pinworm ova are deposited around the anal orifice.

question: Which of the following signs indicates the need for sputum examination for AFB?
rationale: Cough for 3 weeks. A client is considered a PTB suspect when he has cough for 2 weeks or more, plus one or more of the following signs: fever for 1 month or more; chest pain lasting for 2 weeks or more not attributed to other conditions; progressive, unexplained weight loss; night sweats; and hemoptysis.

question: Which clients are considered targets for DOTS Category I?

choices.C: Relapses and failures of previous PTB treatment regimens
choices.D: lients diagnosed for the first time through a positive sputum exam

rationale: Clients diagnosed for the first time through a positive sputum exam. Category I is for new clients diagnosed by sputum examination and clients diagnosed to have a serious form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, such as TB osteomyelitis.

question: To improve compliance to treatment, what innovation is being implemented in DOTS?

choices.A: Having the health worker follow up the client at home
choices.B: Having the health worker or a responsible family member monitor drug intake
choices.C: Having the patient come to the health center every month to get his medications
choices.D: Having a target list to check on whether the patient has collected his monthly supply of drugs

rationale: Having the health worker or a responsible family member monitor drug intake. Directly Observed Treatment Short Course is so-called because a treatment partner, preferably a health worker accessible to the client, monitors the client’s compliance to the treatment.

question: Diagnosis of leprosy is highly dependent on recognition of symptoms. Which of the following is an early sign of leprosy?
rationale: Thickened painful nerves. The lesion of leprosy is not macular. It is characterized by a change in skin color (either reddish or whitish) and loss of sensation, sweating and hair growth over the lesion. Inability to close the eyelids (lagophthalmos) and sinking of the nosebridge are late symptoms.

question: Which of the following clients should be classified as a case of multibacillary leprosy?

choices.A: 3 skin lesions, negative slit skin smear
choices.B: 3 skin lesions, positive slit skin smear
choices.C: 5 skin lesions, negative slit skin smear
choices.D: 5 skin lesions, positive slit skin smear

rationale: 5 skin lesions, positive slit skin smear. A multibacillary leprosy case is one who has a positive slit skin smear and at least 5 skin lesions.
